absent: Numeric values and bit positions for tick dependency bits and masks.
Complete layouts of tick scheduler, task, signal, timer base, timekeeper and migration structures beyond named fields.
Semantics of RCU, interrupt work, softirq, high-resolution timer and clock-event facilities.
Wheel geometry constants and maximum timer delta value.
Timekeeping clock idle limit selection and sequence consistency beyond observed read retry.
Migration hierarchy group formation and walk callback effects.
Boot mask allocation failure behavior and mask lifetime.
Scheduler queueing, CPU assignment and preemption control contracts.
Trace event payloads for tick stop and timer idle transitions.
Jiffy update and watchdog effects during idle wake.

findings.text: Global tick dependency control records or releases a dependency bit in a process-wide mask; first active bit wakes all online full tickless CPUs while release is silent.

Per-CPU dependency control records or releases a bit in the target CPU scheduler state; first activation requests local or remote restart with a guard against remote use in non-maskable context, release never wakes.
Per-task and per-process dependency controls record or release a bit in task or shared signal state; first activation nudges affected queued tasks, with the process variant covering member threads.

Kick interfaces offer self, single-CPU and task-switch driven restart requests for stopped full tickless operation through per-CPU hard interrupt work whose handler leaves actual restart to interrupt exit.
Query interfaces expose whether a CPU tick is stopped, the allowable timekeeping deferment horizon, and the next timer interrupt horizon used for idle planning.
Boot establishes the full tickless CPU set and running state, offers a boolean switch for tickless operation, and vetoes offline transition of the timekeeping CPU while full mode runs.
Full tick cessation is allowed only on an online CPU with no dependency indicated in any of the global, per-CPU, current task and current process masks.

Dependency presence derives from an atomic mask, using a fast whole-word test when stop tracing is off and per-category reporting when tracing is on, covering timer, performance, scheduler, clock stability and RCU concerns.

Full tick stop evaluation and jiffies catch-up both run with interrupts controlled locally, with stop evaluation requiring them already disabled and catch-up saving and restoring them around the time update.
Timer horizon query orders the local timer base lock before the global base lock with nesting and releases in reverse, while migration CPU updates serialize on the migration CPU lock.
Process-wide dependency activation requires the caller to already hold the shared signal lock while visiting member threads.

Per-CPU tick scheduler state carries a dependency mask, stopped and high-resolution and last-do-timer flags, plus last tick, cached next tick, jiffy snapshot, timer base and horizon fields and a scheduler timer.

Timer bases carry a clock, cached next expiry with recalculation and pending indicators, a pending bitmap, idle state, lock and CPU identity; horizon queries produce separate local and global expiry values.
Migration CPU state carries a lock, cached wakeup horizon, current event expiry with ignore and remote markers; a walk carrier conveys new, first and event horizons plus remote scope.

Idle horizon selection prefers a short tick when runtime services or pending soft work require it, otherwise adopts the earliest timer horizon bounded by timekeeping deferment and timekeeping duty, never earlier than base time.

Timer base idle marking engages when the next event lies beyond the immediate tick and coordinates with migration hierarchy handling for idle entry, tick-stop evaluation and fast checks, including reactivation when idle is refused.
Tick restart advances a stale deadline by whole tick periods and reprograms the wakeup through the appropriate high-resolution or clock-event path while clearing cached deadline state.

Remote restart from non-maskable context is rejected with a one-time warning, horizon queries on offline CPUs and inverted base horizons warn, and task nudges skip non-queued tasks while guarding CPU selection against concurrent migration.
When high-resolution timers are disabled, the next high-resolution expiry is folded into the timer horizon with immediate and rounding rules that avoid repeated stop and reprogram cycles.
Cached next expiry reflects the earliest set bucket across wheel levels, with empty bases pushed far into the future to avoid spurious soft wakeups.
A CPU already serving as remote timer handler ignores new local migration timer updates and reports an unbounded horizon.
Tick period, unbounded horizon, soft interrupt index, pinned absolute high-resolution mode and hotplug busy status appear as symbolic ABI values governing expiry arithmetic and programming.
